$$\mathcal L(X)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}[H,X]+\sum_{a=1}^{m}\left(L_aXL_a^*-\frac12\{L_a^*L_a,X\}\right),$$

For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Write $\mathcal{P}$ for the set of all partitions of
$[a,b]$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]]) and put

$$\mathcal{L} \;:=\; \{\, L(f,P) \ : \ P \in \mathcal{P} \,\}, \qquad \mathcal{U} \;:=\; \{\, U(f,P) \ : \ P \in \mathcal{P} \,\}$$

for the sets of lower and of upper Darboux sums ([[def-darboux-sums]]).

### Both extrema exist

**$\mathcal{P}$ is nonempty**: the pair $(1, t)$ with $t_0 := a$ and $t_k := b$
for $k \ge 1$ is a partition of $[a,b]$, since $a < b$. So $\mathcal{L}$ and
$\mathcal{U}$ are nonempty.

**$\mathcal{L}$ is bounded above and $\mathcal{U}$ is bounded below.** Fix any
$Q \in \mathcal{P}$. By claim 2 of [[lem-refinement-inequalities]],
$L(f,P) \le U(f,Q)$ for every $P \in \mathcal{P}$, so $U(f,Q)$ is an upper bound
of $\mathcal{L}$; and $L(f,Q) \le U(f,P)$ for every $P$, so $L(f,Q)$ is a lower
bound of $\mathcal{U}$.

Hence a nonempty set bounded above has a supremum
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and a nonempty set bounded below has an infimum
([[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]]), each unique ([[lem-sup-unique]]).
The **lower** and **upper Darboux integrals** of $f$ over $[a,b]$ are the real
numbers

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;:=\; \sup \mathcal{L} \;=\; \sup_{P} L(f,P), \qquad \overline{\int_a^b} f \;:=\; \inf \mathcal{U} \;=\; \inf_{P} U(f,P) .$$

### The lower integral never exceeds the upper one

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f .$$

Indeed, for each fixed $Q \in \mathcal{P}$ the number $U(f,Q)$ is an upper bound
of $\mathcal{L}$, so the least upper bound satisfies
$\underline{\int_a^b} f \le U(f,Q)$. As $Q$ was arbitrary, $\underline{\int_a^b}f$
is a lower bound of $\mathcal{U}$, and the greatest lower bound satisfies
$\underline{\int_a^b} f \le \overline{\int_a^b} f$ ([[def-infimum]]).

Moreover, for **every** partition $P$,

$$L(f,P) \;\le\; \underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; U(f,P) ,$$

the outer inequalities because a member of a set is at most its supremum and at
least its infimum.

### Integrability

$f$ is **Darboux integrable on $[a,b]$**, and on this page simply
**integrable**, when

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;=\; \overline{\int_a^b} f ,$$

and then the common value is written

$$\int_a^b f \qquad \text{or} \qquad \int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x ,$$

the **integral of $f$ over $[a,b]$**. It is a single well-determined real
number, being the common value of two numbers each of which is unique
([[lem-sup-unique]]). Without the displayed equality the symbol $\int_a^b f$ is
not defined and is never written.

**The inequality above is the whole difficulty.** By the previous paragraph
integrability is *never* a question of one integral exceeding the other, only of
the gap $\overline{\int_a^b} f - \underline{\int_a^b} f \ge 0$ being $0$; and by
[[thm-riemann-criterion]] that gap is $0$ exactly when a single partition can be
found making $U(f,P) - L(f,P)$ small. Whether that is possible is settled
completely, in terms of the discontinuities of $f$, by
[[thm-lebesgue-criterion]].

**"Riemann integrable" means the same thing here.** The definition above is
Darboux's. Riemann's own definition, in terms of tagged partitions of small
mesh, is [[def-tagged-partition-and-riemann-sum]], and the two define the same
class of functions with the same integral by [[thm-darboux-equals-riemann]].
Until that theorem is proved the two phrases are kept apart; after it they are
used interchangeably, as they are throughout the literature.

Work with finite-dimensional system and environment spaces $H_S=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_E=\mathbb C^m$, where $d,m\geq1$, using the ordered tensor product $H_S\otimes H_E$ with the system factor first. A system or environment state is a positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix of trace one; these state matrices are dimensionless. At the initial time, for every allowed system state $\rho$, adopt the joint preparation $\rho\otimes\eta$, where the fixed environment state $\eta$ does not depend on $\rho$. For each $t\geq0$, choose a declared unitary $U_t$ on $H_S\otimes H_E$, meaning $U_t^*U_t=U_tU_t^*=I$, with $U_0=I$. Work with finite-dimensional system and environment spaces $H_S=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_E=\mathbb C^m$, where $d,m\geq1$, using the ordered tensor product $H_S\otimes H_E$ with the system factor first. A system or environment state is a positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix of trace one; these state matrices are dimensionless. At the initial time, for every allowed system state $\rho$, adopt the joint preparation $\rho\otimes\eta$, where the fixed environment state $\eta$ does not depend on $\rho$. For each $t\geq0$, choose a declared unitary $U_t$ on $H_S\otimes H_E$, meaning $U_t^*U_t=U_tU_t^*=I$, with $U_0=I$. The reduced system dynamics is the map $\Phi_t(\rho)=\operatorname{Tr}_E\!\left(U_t(\rho\otimes\eta)U_t^*\right)$, where for the fixed product basis the finite partial trace has entries $(\operatorname{Tr}_E R)_{\alpha\beta}=\sum_{j=1}^mR_{(\alpha,j),(\beta,j)}$. This assignment excludes initially correlated joint states. It imposes no one-parameter group, continuity, or semigroup law on $U_t$.

A time-homogeneous finite GKSL model may instead be selected as a separate approximation: choose a fixed finite-dimensional Hamiltonian matrix $H=H^*$ in joules, a constant $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds, and finitely many jump matrices $L_a$ in $\mathrm{s}^{-1/2}$, and use $T_t=e^{t\mathcal L}$ for $t\geq0$ with $\mathcal L(X)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}[H,X]+\sum_a\left(L_aXL_a^*-\frac12\{L_a^*L_a,X\}\right)$. Each application must state its rates and physical regime. Selecting this approximation is not a consequence of the finite unitary reduction, and this postulate claims no weak-coupling or reservoir limit.

$$\mathcal L(X)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}[H,X]+\sum_{a=1}^{m}\left(L_aXL_a^*-\frac12\{L_a^*L_a,X\}\right),$$

where $[A,B]=AB-BA$, $\{A,B\}=AB+BA$, and $A^*$ is the conjugate transpose. Each summand has units ${\rm s}^{-1}$ times the units of $X$. An empty sum when $m=0$ is zero. The resulting $\mathcal L$ is a linear map on the matrix space used in the finite-channel definition [[def-qsm-dt-channel-definition]].

For a compact time interval $I\subset\mathbb R$ whose coordinate is time in seconds, continuous functions $H:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $L_a:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ with $H(t)=H(t)^*$ define the corresponding **continuous finite GKSL family** $\mathcal L_t$ by the same formula at each $t$. Let $d\geq1$, let $r\geq0$ be an integer, let $H=H^*\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ have units joules, let $\hbar>0$ have units joule-seconds, and let $L_1,\ldots,L_r\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ have units $\mathrm{s}^{-1/2}$, with the finite GKSL convention of [[def-qsm-dt-gksl-definition]]. For a density matrix $\rho\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, meaning $\rho=\rho^*\geq0$ and $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, define the no-jump branch at time $t\geq0$ by $W_{\varnothing,\varnothing}(t)=R(t)$ and its branch state by $W_{\varnothing,\varnothing}(t)\rho W_{\varnothing,\varnothing}(t)^*$.

All time variables $u,t,s_1,\ldots,s_n$ are measured in seconds. Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Write $\mathcal{P}$ for the set of all partitions of
$[a,b]$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]]) and put

$$\mathcal{L} \;:=\; \{\, L(f,P) \ : \ P \in \mathcal{P} \,\}, \qquad \mathcal{U} \;:=\; \{\, U(f,P) \ : \ P \in \mathcal{P} \,\}$$

for the sets of lower and of upper Darboux sums ([[def-darboux-sums]]).

### Both extrema exist

**$\mathcal{P}$ is nonempty**: the pair $(1, t)$ with $t_0 := a$ and $t_k := b$
for $k \ge 1$ is a partition of $[a,b]$, since $a < b$. So $\mathcal{L}$ and
$\mathcal{U}$ are nonempty.

**$\mathcal{L}$ is bounded above and $\mathcal{U}$ is bounded below.** Fix any
$Q \in \mathcal{P}$. By claim 2 of [[lem-refinement-inequalities]],
$L(f,P) \le U(f,Q)$ for every $P \in \mathcal{P}$, so $U(f,Q)$ is an upper bound
of $\mathcal{L}$; and $L(f,Q) \le U(f,P)$ for every $P$, so $L(f,Q)$ is a lower
bound of $\mathcal{U}$.

Hence a nonempty set bounded above has a supremum
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and a nonempty set bounded below has an infimum
([[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]]), each unique ([[lem-sup-unique]]).
The **lower** and **upper Darboux integrals** of $f$ over $[a,b]$ are the real
numbers

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;:=\; \sup \mathcal{L} \;=\; \sup_{P} L(f,P), \qquad \overline{\int_a^b} f \;:=\; \inf \mathcal{U} \;=\; \inf_{P} U(f,P) .$$

### The lower integral never exceeds the upper one

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f .$$

Indeed, for each fixed $Q \in \mathcal{P}$ the number $U(f,Q)$ is an upper bound
of $\mathcal{L}$, so the least upper bound satisfies
$\underline{\int_a^b} f \le U(f,Q)$. As $Q$ was arbitrary, $\underline{\int_a^b}f$
is a lower bound of $\mathcal{U}$, and the greatest lower bound satisfies
$\underline{\int_a^b} f \le \overline{\int_a^b} f$ ([[def-infimum]]).

Moreover, for **every** partition $P$,

$$L(f,P) \;\le\; \underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; U(f,P) ,$$

the outer inequalities because a member of a set is at most its supremum and at
least its infimum.

### Integrability

$f$ is **Darboux integrable on $[a,b]$**, and on this page simply
**integrable**, when

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;=\; \overline{\int_a^b} f ,$$

and then the common value is written

$$\int_a^b f \qquad \text{or} \qquad \int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x ,$$

the **integral of $f$ over $[a,b]$**. It is a single well-determined real
number, being the common value of two numbers each of which is unique
([[lem-sup-unique]]). Without the displayed equality the symbol $\int_a^b f$ is
not defined and is never written.

**The inequality above is the whole difficulty.** By the previous paragraph
integrability is *never* a question of one integral exceeding the other, only of
the gap $\overline{\int_a^b} f - \underline{\int_a^b} f \ge 0$ being $0$; and by
[[thm-riemann-criterion]] that gap is $0$ exactly when a single partition can be
found making $U(f,P) - L(f,P)$ small. Whether that is possible is settled
completely, in terms of the discontinuities of $f$, by
[[thm-lebesgue-criterion]].

**"Riemann integrable" means the same thing here.** The definition above is
Darboux's. Riemann's own definition, in terms of tagged partitions of small
mesh, is [[def-tagged-partition-and-riemann-sum]], and the two define the same
class of functions with the same integral by [[thm-darboux-equals-riemann]].
Until that theorem is proved the two phrases are kept apart; after it they are
used interchangeably, as they are throughout the literature.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
(Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point). Then $f$ is bounded (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

Fix a finite dimension $d\geq1$, a positive constant $\hbar$ in joule-seconds, a Hermitian matrix $H\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ in joules, and a finite family $L_1,\ldots,L_m\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ with units ${\rm s}^{-1/2}$, where $m\geq0$. On dimensionless matrices $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, define the **finite Gorini–Kossakowski–Sudarshan–Lindblad (GKSL) generator**

$$\mathcal L(X)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}[H,X]+\sum_{a=1}^{m}\left(L_aXL_a^*-\frac12\{L_a^*L_a,X\}\right),$$

where $[A,B]=AB-BA$, $\{A,B\}=AB+BA$, and $A^*$ is the conjugate transpose. Each summand has units ${\rm s}^{-1}$ times the units of $X$. An empty sum when $m=0$ is zero. The resulting $\mathcal L$ is a linear map on the matrix space used in the finite-channel definition [[def-qsm-dt-channel-definition]].

For a compact time interval $I\subset\mathbb R$ whose coordinate is time in seconds, continuous functions $H:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $L_a:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ with $H(t)=H(t)^*$ define the corresponding **continuous finite GKSL family** $\mathcal L_t$ by the same formula at each $t$. A propagator for this family means a family of linear maps $\Lambda(t,s)$, $s\leq t$ in $I$, satisfying $\partial_t\Lambda(t,s)=\mathcal L_t\circ\Lambda(t,s)$ and $\Lambda(s,s)=\operatorname{id}$. This definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

These are finite-dimensional mathematical definitions. They do not assert that a physical system follows this generator or that a microscopic bath has a Markovian limit.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Write $\mathcal{P}$ for the set of all partitions of
$[a,b]$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]]) and put

$$\mathcal{L} \;:=\; \{\, L(f,P) \ : \ P \in \mathcal{P} \,\}, \qquad \mathcal{U} \;:=\; \{\, U(f,P) \ : \ P \in \mathcal{P} \,\}$$

for the sets of lower and of upper Darboux sums ([[def-darboux-sums]]).

### Both extrema exist

**$\mathcal{P}$ is nonempty**: the pair $(1, t)$ with $t_0 := a$ and $t_k := b$
for $k \ge 1$ is a partition of $[a,b]$, since $a < b$. So $\mathcal{L}$ and
$\mathcal{U}$ are nonempty.

**$\mathcal{L}$ is bounded above and $\mathcal{U}$ is bounded below.** Fix any
$Q \in \mathcal{P}$. By claim 2 of [[lem-refinement-inequalities]],
$L(f,P) \le U(f,Q)$ for every $P \in \mathcal{P}$, so $U(f,Q)$ is an upper bound
of $\mathcal{L}$; and $L(f,Q) \le U(f,P)$ for every $P$, so $L(f,Q)$ is a lower
bound of $\mathcal{U}$.

Hence a nonempty set bounded above has a supremum
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and a nonempty set bounded below has an infimum
([[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]]), each unique ([[lem-sup-unique]]).
The **lower** and **upper Darboux integrals** of $f$ over $[a,b]$ are the real
numbers

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;:=\; \sup \mathcal{L} \;=\; \sup_{P} L(f,P), \qquad \overline{\int_a^b} f \;:=\; \inf \mathcal{U} \;=\; \inf_{P} U(f,P) .$$

### The lower integral never exceeds the upper one

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f .$$

Indeed, for each fixed $Q \in \mathcal{P}$ the number $U(f,Q)$ is an upper bound
of $\mathcal{L}$, so the least upper bound satisfies
$\underline{\int_a^b} f \le U(f,Q)$. As $Q$ was arbitrary, $\underline{\int_a^b}f$
is a lower bound of $\mathcal{U}$, and the greatest lower bound satisfies
$\underline{\int_a^b} f \le \overline{\int_a^b} f$ ([[def-infimum]]).

Moreover, for **every** partition $P$,

$$L(f,P) \;\le\; \underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; U(f,P) ,$$

the outer inequalities because a member of a set is at most its supremum and at
least its infimum.

### Integrability

$f$ is **Darboux integrable on $[a,b]$**, and on this page simply
**integrable**, when

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;=\; \overline{\int_a^b} f ,$$

and then the common value is written

$$\int_a^b f \qquad \text{or} \qquad \int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x ,$$

the **integral of $f$ over $[a,b]$**. It is a single well-determined real
number, being the common value of two numbers each of which is unique
([[lem-sup-unique]]). Without the displayed equality the symbol $\int_a^b f$ is
not defined and is never written.

**The inequality above is the whole difficulty.** By the previous paragraph
integrability is *never* a question of one integral exceeding the other, only of
the gap $\overline{\int_a^b} f - \underline{\int_a^b} f \ge 0$ being $0$; and by
[[thm-riemann-criterion]] that gap is $0$ exactly when a single partition can be
found making $U(f,P) - L(f,P)$ small. Whether that is possible is settled
completely, in terms of the discontinuities of $f$, by
[[thm-lebesgue-criterion]].

**"Riemann integrable" means the same thing here.** The definition above is
Darboux's. Riemann's own definition, in terms of tagged partitions of small
mesh, is [[def-tagged-partition-and-riemann-sum]], and the two define the same
class of functions with the same integral by [[thm-darboux-equals-riemann]].
Until that theorem is proved the two phrases are kept apart; after it they are
used interchangeably, as they are throughout the literature.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
(Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point). Then $f$ is bounded (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Powers are those of Integer powers $a^m$, and $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{R}$ is the canonical natural of The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field, so that
$\iota(0) = 0$ and $\iota(m+1) = \iota(m) + 1$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

1. The function $p_0 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $p_0(x) = x^{0}$, is the
   constant function $1$, and it is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$
   with $p_0'(c) = 0$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set).
2. For $n \ge 1$ the function $p_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $p_n(x) = x^{n}$, is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and
   $$p_n'(c) \;=\; \iota(n)\,c^{\,n-1} .$$
3. For $n \ge 1$ put $A_0 := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ne 0 \,\}$. The function
   $m_n : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $m_n(x) = x^{-n}$, is differentiable at every
   $c \in A_0$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$m_n'(c) \;=\; -\,\iota(n)\,c^{\,-n-1} .$$
4. Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $a_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$, and let
   $P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the polynomial function
   $P(x) = \sum_{j<n} a_j x^{j}$ (Finite sums and finite products, by recursion). Then $P$ is
   differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and, defining $e : \mathbb{N}
   \to \mathbb{R}$ by $e_0 := 0$ and $e_j := \iota(j)\,a_j\,c^{\,j-1}$ for
   $j \ge 1$,
   $$P'(c) \;=\; \sum_{j<n} e_j .$$

**Claim 2 is stated for $n \ge 1$ and not for $n \ge 0$, and that is not
timidity.** At $n = 0$ its right-hand side reads $\iota(0)\,c^{-1}$, and
$c^{-1}$ is not defined at $c = 0$ (Integer powers $a^m$), so the formula is
not a statement about the whole line. Claim 1 is what covers $n = 0$, and it
says the derivative is $0$ there, which is what the informal reading
"$0 \cdot c^{-1}$" is reaching for. The same shift is why the term $e_0$ of
claim 4 is defined to be $0$ outright rather than by the formula.

citations.quote: In the finite product-state model, fix any $t\geq0$ and define the complex-linear map $\Phi_t:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ by $\Phi_t(X)=\operatorname{Tr}_E\!\left(U_t(X\otimes\eta)U_t^*\right)$. Then $\Phi_t$ is a finite quantum channel. The family $t\mapsto\Phi_t$ need not obey the semigroup law and need not be CP-divisible. The terms “semigroup law” and “CP-divisible” have the definitions of [[def-nrqmx-finite-channel-families]].

Let $d\geq1$ and let $\Phi_t:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ be a family of finite quantum channels indexed by $t\geq0$, where “finite quantum channel” has the meaning in [[def-qsm-dt-channel-definition]]. The family obeys the **semigroup law** when $\Phi_0=\operatorname{id}_{M_d(\mathbb C)}$ and $\Phi_{t+s}=\Phi_t\circ\Phi_s$ for every $s,t\geq0$.

The family is **CP-divisible** when for every $0\leq s\leq t$ there exists a finite quantum channel $V_{t,s}:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ such that $\Phi_t=V_{t,s}\circ\Phi_s$. CP-divisibility is this specified factorization property; the definition does not assert that it is a universal meaning of “Markovian”.

The map $t\mapsto(\cos t,\sin t)$ is a bijection from $[0,2\pi)$ onto $S^1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

derivations.claim: In the environment $Z$ eigenbasis $|b\rangle$, $b=\pm1$, the finite spectral calculus [F7] gives $U_t=\sum_{b=\pm1}V_b(t)\otimes|b\rangle\langle b|$ with $V_b(t)=\operatorname{diag}(e^{-ibgt},e^{ibgt})$. By [F4], each diagonal phase has modulus one, so these blocks and $U_t$ are unitary. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. For $\gamma>0$ and a one-jump history at $s\in(0,T)$, $R(T-s)LR(s)|1\rangle=\sqrt{\gamma}\,e^{-(i\omega+\gamma/2)s}|0\rangle$, since $L|1\rangle=\sqrt{\gamma}|0\rangle$ and $R(T-s)|0\rangle=|0\rangle$. Its branch-weight density from [F2] is $\gamma e^{-\gamma s}$. Because $L|0\rangle=0$ and $R(u)|0\rangle=|0\rangle$, every branch with at least two jumps has zero weight. The normalized ensemble [F3] therefore gives $\int_0^T\gamma e^{-\gamma s}\,ds=1-e^{-\gamma T}$: the only nonzero contributions are the no-jump weight $e^{-\gamma T}$ from step 1.1 and the one-jump integral. Letting $T\to\infty$, [F4] identifies this as the real exponential and [F5] gives $e^{-\gamma T}\to0$ because $\gamma>0$; hence the first-jump density has total mass one. Each first jump leaves the normalized state $|0\rangle\langle0|$. If $\gamma=0$, then $L=0$, all positive-jump branches vanish, and the no-jump weight is one.

Put $K=-iH/\hbar-\frac12\sum_{a=1}^rL_a^*L_a$ and $R(u)=e^{uK}$ for $u\geq0$, with the exponential defined by its norm-convergent power series. For a density matrix $\rho\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, meaning $\rho=\rho^*\geq0$ and $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, define the no-jump branch at time $t\geq0$ by $W_{\varnothing,\varnothing}(t)=R(t)$ and its branch state by $W_{\varnothing,\varnothing}(t)\rho W_{\varnothing,\varnothing}(t)^*$.

All time variables $u,t,s_1,\ldots,s_n$ are measured in seconds. For $n\geq1$, a jump-history label is $\mathbf a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in\{1,\ldots,r\}^n$ and its jump times are seconds $0<s_1<\cdots<s_n<t$. Define the corresponding branch operator by $W_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)=R(t-s_n)L_{a_n}R(s_n-s_{n-1})\cdots L_{a_2}R(s_2-s_1)L_{a_1}R(s_1)$ and the unnormalized branch state by $W_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)\rho W_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)^*$. Its branch-weight density is the real-valued scalar function $w_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)=\operatorname{Tr}(W_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)\rho W_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)^*)$. For $n\geq1$, let $\overline{\Delta}_n(t)=\{(s_1,\ldots,s_n)\in\mathbb R^n:0\leq s_1\leq\cdots\leq s_n\leq t\}$ and $\Delta_n(t)=\{(s_1,\ldots,s_n)\in\mathbb R^n:0<s_1<\cdots<s_n<t\}$. Use the same formula for $W_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)$ on $\overline{\Delta}_n(t)$; it is continuous there because $R(u)=e^{uK}$ is continuous for $u\geq0$. If $V$ is a finite-dimensional real or complex vector space and $F:\overline{\Delta}_n(t)\to V$ has continuous coordinates in a basis, define $\int_{\Delta_n(t)}F(\mathbf s)\,d\mathbf s$ as exactly the repeated one-variable Riemann integral over the closed limits shown here $\int_0^t ds_n\int_0^{s_n}ds_{n-1}\cdots\int_0^{s_2}F(s_1,\ldots,s_n)\,ds_1$, integrating each real coordinate; for complex coordinates, integrate their real and imaginary parts separately. This value is independent of the basis because a change of basis is a finite linear combination and scalar Riemann integration is linear. For $V=\mathbb R$ this defines the scalar integral of the density $w_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}(t)$; the same convention applies to branch-state integrands with values in $M_d(\mathbb C)$ and to integrands with values in the finite-dimensional complex vector space of complex-linear maps $M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_d(\mathbb C)$. The full recursion is well-defined for these arbitrary continuous integrands by [[lem-nrqmx-continuous-simplex-integrals]]: every inner integral is continuous in all remaining ordered parameters, so the next integral exists. That lemma also proves basis independence, linear-map commutation, the norm bound by the supremum times $t^n/n!$, and positivity for nonnegative real scalar integrands. Set $\int_a^a f(s)\,ds=0$ for a degenerate interval; hence every $n\geq1$ ordered-simplex integral at $t=0$ is zero. Let $\Delta_0(t)=\{()\}$ and define $\int_{\Delta_0(t)}F=F(())$; in the expansion, the $n=0$ contribution is the no-jump branch already defined above. For $n\geq1$, $W_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}$ has units $\mathrm{s}^{-n/2}$ and $w_{\mathbf a,\mathbf s}$ has units $\mathrm{s}^{-n}$; integrating over the $n$ time variables gives a dimensionless weight. If $r=0$, there are no branches with $n\geq1$. This definition alone does not assert that the branch weights sum to one.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Write $\mathcal{P}$ for the set of all partitions of
$[a,b]$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]]) and put

$$\mathcal{L} \;:=\; \{\, L(f,P) \ : \ P \in \mathcal{P} \,\}, \qquad \mathcal{U} \;:=\; \{\, U(f,P) \ : \ P \in \mathcal{P} \,\}$$

for the sets of lower and of upper Darboux sums ([[def-darboux-sums]]).

### Both extrema exist

**$\mathcal{P}$ is nonempty**: the pair $(1, t)$ with $t_0 := a$ and $t_k := b$
for $k \ge 1$ is a partition of $[a,b]$, since $a < b$. So $\mathcal{L}$ and
$\mathcal{U}$ are nonempty.

**$\mathcal{L}$ is bounded above and $\mathcal{U}$ is bounded below.** Fix any
$Q \in \mathcal{P}$. By claim 2 of [[lem-refinement-inequalities]],
$L(f,P) \le U(f,Q)$ for every $P \in \mathcal{P}$, so $U(f,Q)$ is an upper bound
of $\mathcal{L}$; and $L(f,Q) \le U(f,P)$ for every $P$, so $L(f,Q)$ is a lower
bound of $\mathcal{U}$.

Hence a nonempty set bounded above has a supremum
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and a nonempty set bounded below has an infimum
([[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]]), each unique ([[lem-sup-unique]]).
The **lower** and **upper Darboux integrals** of $f$ over $[a,b]$ are the real
numbers

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;:=\; \sup \mathcal{L} \;=\; \sup_{P} L(f,P), \qquad \overline{\int_a^b} f \;:=\; \inf \mathcal{U} \;=\; \inf_{P} U(f,P) .$$

### The lower integral never exceeds the upper one

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f .$$

Indeed, for each fixed $Q \in \mathcal{P}$ the number $U(f,Q)$ is an upper bound
of $\mathcal{L}$, so the least upper bound satisfies
$\underline{\int_a^b} f \le U(f,Q)$. As $Q$ was arbitrary, $\underline{\int_a^b}f$
is a lower bound of $\mathcal{U}$, and the greatest lower bound satisfies
$\underline{\int_a^b} f \le \overline{\int_a^b} f$ ([[def-infimum]]).

Moreover, for **every** partition $P$,

$$L(f,P) \;\le\; \underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; U(f,P) ,$$

the outer inequalities because a member of a set is at most its supremum and at
least its infimum.

### Integrability

$f$ is **Darboux integrable on $[a,b]$**, and on this page simply
**integrable**, when

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;=\; \overline{\int_a^b} f ,$$

and then the common value is written

$$\int_a^b f \qquad \text{or} \qquad \int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x ,$$

the **integral of $f$ over $[a,b]$**. It is a single well-determined real
number, being the common value of two numbers each of which is unique
([[lem-sup-unique]]). Without the displayed equality the symbol $\int_a^b f$ is
not defined and is never written.

**The inequality above is the whole difficulty.** By the previous paragraph
integrability is *never* a question of one integral exceeding the other, only of
the gap $\overline{\int_a^b} f - \underline{\int_a^b} f \ge 0$ being $0$; and by
[[thm-riemann-criterion]] that gap is $0$ exactly when a single partition can be
found making $U(f,P) - L(f,P)$ small. Whether that is possible is settled
completely, in terms of the discontinuities of $f$, by
[[thm-lebesgue-criterion]].

**"Riemann integrable" means the same thing here.** The definition above is
Darboux's. Riemann's own definition, in terms of tagged partitions of small
mesh, is [[def-tagged-partition-and-riemann-sum]], and the two define the same
class of functions with the same integral by [[thm-darboux-equals-riemann]].
Until that theorem is proved the two phrases are kept apart; after it they are
used interchangeably, as they are throughout the literature.

**Why this item is first.** The published definition of the integral does not
cover this page. [[def-darboux-integral]] is stated for reals $a < b$, because
the partitions it quantifies over are those of [[def-partition-and-refinement]],
whose standing hypothesis is $a < b$: with $a = b$ the chain
$a = t_0 < \dots < t_n = b$ is unsatisfiable. So $\int_a^b f$ is an undefined
symbol whenever $a \ge b$, and every additivity statement below would be
ill-formed as it is usually written. This item extends the notation, and nothing
else: the object it names is still the Darboux integral of
[[def-darboux-integral]].

Let $u, v \in \mathbb{R}$ and write

$$[u \wedge v,\ u \vee v] \;:=\; \text{the closed interval with endpoints } u \text{ and } v$$

([[def-interval]]). Let $f$ be a real-valued function whose domain contains that
interval. Say that **$f$ is integrable between $u$ and $v$** when either $u = v$,
or $u \ne v$ and the restriction of $f$ to $[u \wedge v,\ u \vee v]$ is bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux integrable there ([[def-darboux-integral]],
[[def-darboux-sums]]). For such $f$ define

$$\int_u^v f \;:=\; \begin{cases} \text{the Darboux integral of } f \text{ over } [u,v] & \text{if } u < v, \\[2pt] 0 & \text{if } u = v, \\[2pt] -\displaystyle\int_v^u f & \text{if } u > v. \end{cases}$$

**There is nothing to check for consistency.** The three clauses are indexed by
the three cases of trichotomy, $u < v$, $u = v$ and $u > v$, which are mutually
exclusive and exhaustive; no pair of them ever applies to the same $(u,v)$. In
particular the first clause is untouched, so on $u < v$ this is the published
integral verbatim and every published theorem about it applies unchanged.

**The middle clause is a stipulation, not a computation.** It is *not* claimed
that $0$ is a value forced by the $u < v$ definition in any limiting sense; that
definition simply says nothing at $u = v$, and $\int_u^u f := 0$ is what is
written there. It is also unconditional: no hypothesis on $f$ beyond being
defined at $u$ is asked for, since the case $u = v$ never refers to a partition.

### The two consequences used throughout the page

**Antisymmetry, for every pair.** For all reals $u, v$ with $f$ integrable
between them,

$$\int_u^v f \;=\; -\int_v^u f .$$

Indeed if $u < v$ then $v > u$ and the third clause reads
$\int_v^u f = -\int_u^v f$, which rearranges to the display; if $u = v$ both
sides are $0$; and if $u > v$ the third clause is the display itself.

**Absolute values agree.** Consequently
$\bigl|\int_u^v f\bigr| = \bigl|\int_v^u f\bigr|$ for every such pair.

**An obligation recorded here and discharged elsewhere.** With this convention
the additivity identity

$$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f$$

holds for **every** arrangement of $u, v, w$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable, not only for $u < v < w$. That is a theorem and not part of this
definition; it is proved as the last clause of
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], and nothing on this page uses it before it
is proved there.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
(Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point). Then $f$ is bounded (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. $f + g$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b (f+g) = \int_a^b f + \int_a^b g$;
2. for every real $\lambda$, $\lambda f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b \lambda f = \lambda \int_a^b f$;
3. consequently, for all reals $\lambda, \mu$ the function $\lambda f + \mu g$ is
   integrable and
   $$\int_a^b(\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f \;+\; \mu\int_a^b g ;$$
4. the same identity holds with oriented limits: if $u, v \in [a,b]$ and $f, g$
   are integrable between $u$ and $v$ ([[def-oriented-integral]]), then
   $\int_u^v(\lambda f + \mu g) = \lambda\int_u^v f + \mu\int_u^v g$.

**Linearity of the integral is not linearity of the Darboux sums**, and the
proof of claim 1 has to squeeze rather than compute. On a subinterval the
inequality $\sup(f+g) \le \sup f + \sup g$ can be strict — take $f(x) = x$ and
$g(x) = -x$ on $[0,1]$, where the left side is $0$ and the right side is $1$ —
so $U(f+g,P)$ is in general strictly below $U(f,P) + U(g,P)$ and no identity
between upper sums is available. Claim 2, by contrast, is an identity at the
level of the sums, with the roles of $\sup$ and $\inf$ exchanged when
$\lambda < 0$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
(The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
FALSE: a nonnegative Riemann integrable function on $[a,b]$ with $\int_a^b f = 0$ is identically zero on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is A continuous $f \ge 0$ on $[a,b]$ with $\int_a^b f = 0$ is identically $0$
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of The integral with oriented limits: $\int_a^a f := 0$ and $\int_b^a f := -\int_a^b f$, $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]) and let $I \in \mathbb{R}$. The following are equivalent.

1. **(Darboux)** $f$ is Darboux integrable on $[a,b]$ with
   $\int_a^b f = I$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).
2. **(Riemann)** For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real $\delta > 0$
   such that
   $$\bigl|\,S(f,P,\xi) - I\,\bigr| \;<\; \varepsilon$$
   for **every** tagged partition $(P,\xi)$ of $[a,b]$ with $\|P\| < \delta$
   ([[def-tagged-partition-and-riemann-sum]], [[def-partition-and-refinement]]).

**The quantifier over tagged partitions is universal, and that is the content.**
Condition 2 constrains every tagged partition of small mesh at once, tags
included; it is not a statement about one sequence of tagged partitions, and it
cannot be weakened to one. The companion page of this pair exhibits a
non-integrable function whose Riemann sums are constant along such a sequence.

**Boundedness is a hypothesis of both conditions as stated here.** Condition 1
presupposes it, since the Darboux sums of an unbounded function do not exist
([[def-darboux-sums]]); condition 2 makes sense for unbounded $f$ as well, and
in fact implies boundedness, but that implication is not proved here and is not
used: every application on this page starts from a bounded $f$.

Let $c < d$ be reals and let $\varphi : [c,d] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable
at every point of $[c,d]$ as a function on $[c,d]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), with
$\varphi'$ integrable on $[c,d]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex with at least two elements
(Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) with $\varphi[\,[c,d]\,] \subseteq J$, and let $f : J \to
\mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $J$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point).

Then $(f\circ\varphi)\,\varphi'$ is integrable on $[c,d]$ and

$$\int_{\varphi(c)}^{\varphi(d)} f \;=\; \int_c^d (f\circ\varphi)\,\varphi' ,$$

the left-hand integral being the oriented one of The integral with oriented limits: $\int_a^a f := 0$ and $\int_b^a f := -\int_a^b f$.

**Neither injectivity nor monotonicity of $\varphi$ is assumed**, and that is
exactly why the left-hand side is written with oriented limits: $\varphi(d)$ may
lie below $\varphi(c)$, and $\varphi$ may return to the same value many times.
The proof runs through a primitive of $f$ and the chain rule, and no inverse
function is ever formed.

**Continuity of $f$ is a hypothesis and cannot be weakened to integrability.**
With $f$ merely integrable the composite $f \circ \varphi$ need not be
integrable at all, so the right-hand side need not exist; that is
the false statement that weakens it on the companion page.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous (Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
(Uniform continuity of a map of metric spaces: one $\delta$ serving every point).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
(Every open cover of a compact metric space has a Lebesgue number: a $\delta > 0$ such that every nonempty subset of diameter less than $\delta$ lies inside a single member of the cover).

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Powers are those of Integer powers $a^m$, and $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to

$\iota(0) = 0$ and $\iota(m+1) = \iota(m) + 1$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

1. The function $p_0 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $p_0(x) = x^{0}$, is the

4. Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $a_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$, and let
   $P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the polynomial function
   $P(x) = \sum_{j<n} a_j x^{j}$ (Finite sums and finite products, by recursion). Then $P$ is

timidity.** At $n = 0$ its right-hand side reads $\iota(0)\,c^{-1}$, and

not a statement about the whole line. Claim 1 is what covers $n = 0$, and it

derivations.claim: First consider a continuous curve $g:[a,b]\to V$. In a real basis $e_1,\ldots,e_q$, its coordinate functions are integrable by [F1], and define its integral by their integrals. For a complex basis use the underlying real basis $e_1,ie_1,\ldots,e_q,ie_q$; this is exactly the real-and-imaginary convention. The zero-dimensional space is immediate. In either case the triangle inequality gives $\|\sum_j c_je_j\|\leq\sum_j|c_j|\|e_j\|$. Thus coordinate convergence implies convergence in any chosen norm, without assuming norm equivalence. By [F2], tagged sums of $g$ converge in that norm to its coordinate integral. The reverse triangle inequality and the same finite-coordinate bound show that $s\mapsto\|g(s)\|$ is continuous, so it too is integrable. For each tagged partition, the norm of the vector sum is at most the corresponding sum of the scalar norms. Taking limits by [F2] proves $\|\int_a^b g\|\leq\int_a^b\|g\|$ when $a<b$; for $a=b$ both integrals are zero. A coordinate change or a linear map has entries given by a finite matrix, so scalar linearity [F2] proves that integration commutes with it, and hence proves basis independence. This also proves linearity, and [F2] proves that a nonnegative real curve has nonnegative integral. All statements concern finite lists of coordinates, and require only finitely many simultaneous estimates.

Suppose $G_{k-1}$ is continuous on $D_{n-k+1}(T)$, as is true initially for $G_0=F$. For each $y\in D_{n-k}(T)$, the curve $v\mapsto G_{k-1}(v,y)$ is continuous for $0\leq v\leq b_k(y)$ and is integrable by step 1.1. Set $b=b_k$ and
$$
H(u,y)=G_{k-1}(u b(y),y),\qquad 0\leq u\leq1.
$$
The evaluation map $(u,y)\mapsto(ub(y),y)$ is continuous and lands in $D_{n-k+1}(T)$, because $0\leq ub(y)\leq b(y)$ and the coordinates of $y$ are ordered. Thus $H$ is coordinate-continuous. The parameter domain $[0,1]\times D_{n-k}(T)$ is closed and bounded in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, hence compact by [F4]; when there are no remaining coordinates it is just $[0,1]$. The finite-coordinate inequality of step 1.1 shows that $H$ is also continuous into any chosen norm on $V$. Apply [F4] with the Euclidean metric on the parameter domain and that norm metric on $V$. Uniform continuity gives, as $y\to y_0$ within its parameter domain,
$$
\sup_{0\leq u\leq1}\|H(u,y)-H(u,y_0)\|\longrightarrow0.
$$
Indeed the Euclidean distance from $(u,y)$ to $(u,y_0)$ is $|y-y_0|$, independently of $u$. This conclusion also holds coordinate by coordinate if no norm was initially specified, by using the explicitly defined coordinate norm $\sum_j|c_j|$.

If $b(y)>0$, apply [F3] in each real coordinate with $\phi(u)=ub(y)$ and $f(v)=G_{k-1}(v,y)$ on $[0,b(y)]$. All its scalar continuity and differentiability hypotheses hold, and $\phi'$ is constant and integrable. This gives
$$
G_k(y)=b(y)\int_0^1H(u,y)\,du.
$$
If $b(y)=0$, both sides are zero by [F1], so the same identity holds. By linearity and step 1.1, for any fixed $y_0$ its difference at $y$ satisfies
$$
\|G_k(y)-G_k(y_0)\|\leq T\sup_{0\leq u\leq1}\|H(u,y)-H(u,y_0)\|+|b(y)-b(y_0)|\left\|\int_0^1H(u,y_0)\,du\right\|.
$$
The first term tends to zero by step 2.1 and the second by continuity of $b$. Thus $G_k$ is continuous, including at parameters with $b=0$. If there are no remaining coordinates this is continuity on a singleton. Induction proves existence and continuity at every recursive stage. When $T=0$ and $n\geq1$, already the first integration has equal endpoints, so all later integrals are zero; the specified $n=0$ value needs no integration.

Apply the linearity, linear-map commutation and basis independence of step 1.1 successively at each stage. Every resulting coordinate curve is continuous by step 3.1, so these operations are legitimate at every stage and prove the corresponding claims for $I_n$. Likewise a nonnegative real $F$ has nonnegative $G_1$, then nonnegative $G_2$, and so on by scalar monotonicity. No exchange of integration order or assertion of differentiability is involved.

Suppose $\|F\|\leq C$. At the first stage step 1.1 and scalar monotonicity give $\|G_1(y)\|\leq C b_1(y)$. If $k\geq2$ and the previous bound is $\|G_{k-1}(s_k,y)\|\leq C s_k^{k-1}/(k-1)!$, the same integral inequality bounds $\|G_k(y)\|$ by $\int_0^{b_k(y)} C v^{k-1}/(k-1)!\,dv=C b_k(y)^k/k!$. The monomial primitive and integral evaluation follow from [F1] and [F5] when the endpoint is positive; equal endpoints give the same value zero. Induction gives the stated final bound. For scalar $F=1$ the same recursion is an equality at every stage, yielding $I_n(1)=T^n/n!$. For $n=0$ both assertions follow directly from $I_0(F)=F(())$ and the factor convention.
